```{r setup}
library(MATH4753THOMASF26)
```

# The data

`freethrows` holds the number of free throws made in each of 50 practice
sessions, with 10 shots per session.

```{r}
head(freethrows)
```

# binFit(): does real data look binomial?

In Lab 5 we only simulated from a known p. `binFit()` starts from observed
data instead. It estimates p from the data, then compares the observed
proportions to the binomial probabilities from `dbinom()`.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
fit = binFit(freethrows$made, n = 10)
fit
```

# binSim(): simulation checked against dbinom()

In Lab 5 Task 2 we ran `mybin()`, then called `dbinom()` separately and
compared the numbers by hand. `binSim()` does both in one call. Here we
simulate using the p estimated from the free throw data.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
sim = binSim(iter = 10000, n = 10, p = fit$p.hat)
sim
```

The largest difference between the simulated and exact values is
`r round(sim$max.difference, 4)`, so the simulation matches the exact
binomial probabilities closely.
